# Choosing a Strategy

After this page you can write a short default for `desk-api` and know where this book will enforce it later.

```text
 versions in the wild? ── yes ──► Git Flow (main + develop + release/*)
        │
        no
        ▼
 several merges/day + flags? ── yes ──► trunk-based
        │
        no
        ▼
 GitHub Flow     short feat/* off main     ← desk default
```

## A default for this book’s desk

- **Topology:** GitHub Flow — short `feat/` / `fix/` branches off `main`, delete after integrate
- **Integrate:** rebase the feature onto `main`, then `--ff-only` or a forge squash
- **`main`:** always deployable; revert to undo (never rebase published `main`)
- **Repos:** polyrepo (`desk-web`, `desk-api`, `desk-infra`) until a chapter says otherwise
- **Host:** Linux; hooks and CI run there first

Write it in `README.md` or `CONTRIBUTING.md` in the repo. A strategy that exists only in someone’s head is not a strategy.

## When to change it

- Multiple supported versions in production → Git Flow release branches
- Several merges to `main` per engineer per day and strong tests → trunk-based plus flags
- One PR always touches all three desks → consider a monorepo
- A compliance officer needs a merge commit per change → `--no-ff` on `main`

## What Git will not decide

Git will merge whatever you ask. Forges add buttons (squash, rebase, merge). Chapter 31 is branch protection, code owners, required checks. This chapter is the **agreement**. The next part (power skills) is internals, reflog, bisect, and repair — the tools you want when the agreement meets a bad Tuesday.
